Description

When reading a packet, russh took the 4-byte packet length sent by the peer and sized its receive buffer from it without any upper bound. The length is fully controlled by the other side of the connection and is read before authentication, so an unauthenticated client can claim packets of up to about 4 GiB and make a server allocate that much memory per connection. A few such connections are enough to run the process out of memory.

From 0.44.1, lengths above 256 KiB are rejected with Error::PacketSize before the buffer is sized.

Description

Many of russh's client and server message handlers decoded length-prefixed strings, byte fields and name-lists from the peer into owned String, Vec or name-list values first and only checked their size and meaning afterwards. This includes the algorithm name-lists in SSH_MSG_KEXINIT, which a server parses during the initial key exchange, before any authentication.

A peer can fill these fields with oversized or highly fragmented values, for example a name-list of hundreds of thousands of one-letter algorithm names, and make russh allocate far more memory than the packet itself takes. With many concurrent connections this can exhaust the memory of a server process.

From 0.61.0, name-lists are rejected before they are split into separate strings when they are longer than 16 KiB or hold more than 1,024 entries, and the key exchange decodes its algorithm lists through this bounded decoder.

Unaffected

Description

With zlib or zlib@openssh.com compression negotiated, the packet length that russh checks applies to the compressed payload only. The decompressor kept growing its output buffer until the whole payload was inflated, with no limit of its own, so a packet that is small on the wire could expand to hundreds of megabytes before it was parsed.

The default server configuration offers both zlib methods, and a client that lists compression first can select it during the initial key exchange. That client can then send such a packet after NEWKEYS but before authenticating, so a russh server with default settings can be made to use large amounts of memory by an unauthenticated peer. A malicious server can do the same to a client that negotiated compression.

From 0.61.1, decompressed output is capped at the same maximum as an uncompressed packet (256 KiB plus a few bytes of header room), and larger packets are rejected with Error::PacketSize.

Description

A server that answers a keyboard-interactive authentication request with prompts (Auth::Partial, as a TOTP or other second-factor login does) then parses the client's SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_INFO_RESPONSE. russh read the number of responses from that message and reserved a vector of that many entries before reading any of them. Servers whose handler keeps the default behaviour, which rejects keyboard-interactive authentication, are not affected. From 0.60.1 the count is limited by how many responses the remaining packet data could actually hold.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0495: Vulnerability in russh
entry.summary: Agent server signs with confirm-constrained keys without calling `Agent::confirm`
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0495

Agent server signs with confirm-constrained keys without calling Agent::confirm
Reported
October 30, 2026
Issued
November 12, 2026
Package
russh (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Keywords
#ssh-agent #confirm #constraint #authorization
Aliases
  • CVE-2026-116794
  • GHSA-vp5q-ff62-jwqv
References
  • https://github.com/Eugeny/russh/commit/62db6e7defd6d244159da962ccccb029e785ce0f
Patched
  • >=0.65.0
Unaffected
  • <0.50.0-beta.12

Description

A key added to an SSH agent with the confirm constraint (what ssh-add -c sends) must not be used to sign until the user approves each use. russh's agent server (russh::keys::agent::server) accepted the constraint, but when a sign request arrived for such a key it used a fixed true in place of the result of Agent::confirm, so the application's confirmation step never ran. This started in 0.50.0-beta.12; 0.50.0-beta.8 to beta.11 still called confirm, and earlier russh releases have no agent server.

Any process that can reach the agent, including a remote host when the agent is forwarded, can then sign with the protected key without the user's approval, for example to log in elsewhere as the user. The private key itself is not disclosed. Agents whose Agent::confirm keeps the default, which always returns true, behave the same before and after the fix.

From 0.65.0 the agent server calls Agent::confirm for confirm-constrained keys and refuses to sign when it returns false. Implementations that left confirm unimplemented (for example as todo!()) will now reach that code.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

Description

On the client side, russh passed channel messages from the server (data, extended data, EOF, close, success, failure, open failure and the exit-status, exit-signal and xon-xoff requests) to the application's client::Handler callbacks without checking that the channel number belonged to a channel the client had opened and the server had confirmed. The server side already performed this check.

A malicious or compromised SSH server can therefore send these messages for any channel number, including the next number the client will allocate (they are assigned in order) or one it has already closed. An application that tracks per-channel state can be made to record a false exit status, see a channel close before its real output arrives, or panic when it looks up a channel it does not know.

From 0.63.1 the client ignores channel messages for channels that are not established and confirmed, and handles an open failure only for a channel it is actually opening.

Panic when decoding malformed Ed25519 keys from Base64

References

Patched
  • >=0.11.2
Affected Functions
Version
vodozemac::Ed25519PublicKey::from_base64
  • <0.11.2
vodozemac::Ed25519SecretKey::from_base64
  • <0.11.2

Description

In version 0.11.1 and earlier of vodozemac, Ed25519PublicKey::from_base64() and Ed25519SecretKey::from_base64() panic on malformed input instead of returning an error, if the input decodes to 31 or 33 bytes instead of the expected 32 bytes. An attacker who can supply a key to an application using vodozemac can crash it.

Impact

Ed25519 public keys are routinely received from other Matrix users and servers, so a malicious party can publish a crafted key that crashes clients parsing it.

The impact is limited to denial of service; no key disclosure or signature forgery is possible.

Description

Beef::merge_raw_tx and BeefTx::from_raw_tx accept raw bytes without a Result. For bytes that are not exactly one transaction (a transaction followed by bytes, a cut transaction, bytes that are no transaction at all), Beef::sort_txs, verify_structure, verify_valid and is_valid could answer valid, even with no BUMP and no parent in the BEEF, and, where the entry carried a BUMP index, treat the hash of those bytes as a proven transaction id; an entry that names it as a parent was answered valid too.

The wire readers (Beef::from_binary, verify_stream, Transaction::from_beef, from_atomic_beef) parse every entry and are not affected. Reaching this needs an application that passes bytes it did not parse to merge_raw_tx or BeefTx::from_raw_tx and then relies on the verdict or on the transaction the BEEF hands back.

0.8.5 refuses such an entry at all four verdict doors, with or without a BUMP index, and every entry that names it as a parent. Where upgrading is not possible, do not rely on is_valid or verify_valid alone for such an entry: check that the bytes are exactly one transaction before merging them.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

Description

Signature::from_der read a DER-encoded ECDSA signature leniently. It read as the signature: the signature followed by other bytes; a sequence length shorter than its contents, or longer with bytes after them (a length byte with its high bit set among them); and an R or S preceded by a zero byte it did not need. Given one signature a key holder made, anyone could produce other byte strings that verify as that signature over the same data. No form verifies over other data: an application that acts on the verdict alone is not affected; one that compares, hashes or stores a signature's bytes is.

0.8.6 refuses each form as Error::InvalidSignature. A signature's bytes are still not unique after the patch: the same signature with S replaced by n - S verifies, so an application that keys on the bytes also requires Signature::is_low_s().

Someone who controls any DNSSEC-signed zone can publish a signed NSEC3 record whose first label is the hash of a name in another zone. An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can then use it to make the validator accept that the name in the other zone does not exist.

This affects DNSSEC validation through DnssecDnsHandle when built with dnssec-ring or dnssec-aws-lc-rs.

The fix requires a matching NSEC3 record to belong to a zone that contains the checked name, and ignores NSEC3 records whose owner is not directly below the RRSIG signer name. It is in 0.26.2.

Description

When extracting archives, eazip validates symlink entries before writing them. The validation function validate_symlink() (src/utils/mod.rs) scans for backslash and NUL bytes, but passes the symlink's name where the symlink's target was intended:

memchr2(b'\\', b'\0', name.as_bytes()) // should be target.as_bytes()

As a result, symlink targets containing backslash or NUL bytes pass validation. On Windows, backslash is a path separator, so targets such as ..\..\..\Windows\system32\evil.exe also defeat the remaining depth check, which splits on / only. A crafted archive can therefore create symlinks that resolve outside the extraction directory — including UNC targets such as \\host\share\... — redirecting writes to arbitrary filesystem locations chosen by the attacker.

Applications that extract untrusted archives with eazip on Windows targets are affected; on Unix targets backslash is not a separator, which limits exposure there.

The vulnerability was introduced in version 0.2.5 and fixed in 0.2.7 (a1phyr/eazip@0e4caa13), which rejects backslash and NUL bytes in the symlink target. It was privately reported to the maintainer on 2026-11-06 and credited in the 0.2.7 release notes.

Description

cap-primitives resolves a path inside a sandboxed directory one component at a time and opens the last component with O_NOFOLLOW, so that a symlink there cannot lead out of the directory. When the path ended in /, the resolver added the slash back to the last component before opening it. With a trailing slash the operating system no longer treats that component as the last one, so O_NOFOLLOW does not apply, the symlink is followed, and the resulting file descriptor was returned without further checks.

A symlink inside the sandbox that points outside it, such as escape -> ../outside or a link to /, can therefore be opened as escape/. If the symlink's own target ends in /, the caller's path does not need a trailing slash at all, so removing trailing slashes from untrusted input is not a workaround. The maintainers' advisory reports reads and writes outside the sandbox through open, open_dir, read_dir and canonicalize, and directory creation, removal and renames outside it through create_dir, remove_dir and rename.

This resolver is used on Windows and macOS, on FreeBSD when O_RESOLVE_BENEATH is not available, and on Linux when openat2 is not available (kernels before 5.6, or a seccomp policy that rejects it). cap-std and other crates built on cap-primitives are affected through it. Wasmtime's WASI filesystem support was affected as well; that is covered by RUSTSEC-2026-0269.

The fix stops re-adding the trailing slash and is in 3.4.6 and 4.0.3.

Description

The extended-attribute functions in rustix::fs (getxattr, lgetxattr, fgetxattr, listxattr, llistxattr and flistxattr) write into a Buffer and then mark as many bytes initialized as the system call reported. When the buffer has zero length, the operating system treats the call as a size query: it writes nothing and returns the size of the attribute value or of the name list. rustix still marked that many bytes as initialized.

Passing a Vec whose length equals its capacity through spare_capacity gives such a zero-length buffer, and rustix then set the vector's length past its capacity over memory that was never written. This is undefined behavior reachable from safe code. With an empty &mut [MaybeUninit<u8>] the call panics instead.

From 1.1.6 these functions return an empty result for a zero-length buffer, and new getxattr_query, lgetxattr_query, fgetxattr_query, listxattr_query, llistxattr_query and flistxattr_query functions return the size. The 0.38 series did not have the Buffer API and is not affected.

Patched

Unaffected
  • <2.0.0

Description

From 2.0.0 until 3.7.0, the rmcp OAuth client decided whether it may fetch an authorization server's metadata URL by inspecting only the host string. It rejected literal loopback, private and link-local IP addresses and known cloud metadata hostnames, but it did not resolve other hostnames. A hostname that resolves to an internal address passed the check.

A malicious MCP server can return protected-resource metadata that names an authorization server whose hostname resolves to an internal address. The client then sends GET requests to that address during discovery.

The same release fixes two related bypasses:

  • Bracketed IPv6 literals such as http://[::1]:6379/ were not recognized as internal, because the check kept the brackets from the URL host.
  • token_endpoint and registration_endpoint from authorization server metadata were not checked at all, and token requests follow redirects. A malicious authorization server could make the client send POST requests to an internal address.

The impact is client-side SSRF. Responses are not returned to the attacker directly. Unauthenticated internal HTTP services are reachable. Cloud metadata endpoints that require headers or IMDSv2 are largely unaffected.

The flaw was corrected in 3.7.0. AuthorizationManager::new now builds its HTTP client with a DNS resolver that applies the address policy to every resolved address, and checks every IP-literal URL and followed redirect against the same policy. Loopback and private addresses are allowed only when the MCP server's own URL names one of that class. Deployments that reach their authorization server through a hostname that resolves to a private address should use AuthorizationManager::new_allowing_private_addresses.

Clients supplied through new_with_oauth_http_client are not covered by the resolved-address checks. Such clients must enforce their own outbound address policy.

Description

When ocipkg unpacks an OCI archive, the destination directory is derived from the image name, which ocipkg reads from the archive's own index.json (org.opencontainers.image.ref.name). That name is attacker-controlled, and ImageName::parse accepts a hostname of .., so the computed destination escapes the local image store. A "zip-slip"-style path traversal (CWE-22 / CWE-23). This is esclatable to code execution.

In Artifact::unpack (src/image/artifact.rs), the destination is image_dir(name) = data_dir().join(name.as_path()) (src/local/mod.rs:31), where the name comes from get_name_from_index (src/image/layout.rs:114-124):

let image_name = self.base.get_name()?;   // from the archive's index.json ref.name
let dest = image_dir(&image_name)?;        // data_dir().join(name.as_path()); hostname ".." escapes
if dest.exists() {
    if overwrite {
        fs::remove_dir_all(&dest)?;        // deletes a directory OUTSIDE the store
    }
}
fs::create_dir_all(&dest)?;
// ... each tar layer is then unpacked under `dest` (also outside the store)

The fix

Fixed in ocipkg 0.4.1 by PR #223. The leading reference component is validated against the org.opencontainers.image.ref.name grammar from OCI Image Specification 1.1.1 on parse and deserialization, and local::image_dir revalidates the name and rejects any non-normal path component (e.g. ..) before any filesystem mutation, so a crafted archive can no longer escape the local image store.

Description

Affected versions of KeyVaultAuthorizer::on_challenge cache the authentication scope from a WWW-Authenticate response before verifying that the challenge resource matches the requested endpoint. When verification rejects the challenge, the scope remains cached. A subsequent request through the same client uses that scope to authorize the request without repeating challenge resource verification.

For azure_security_keyvault_certificates, the affected versions are 0.9.0 through 1.0.0, inclusive, and 1.1.0-beta.1. Versions before 0.9.0 do not use this challenge-scope cache and are unaffected by this issue.

Impact

An application that sends requests to an attacker-controlled endpoint and reuses the same client after a rejected challenge can disclose a bearer token and request body to that endpoint, if its credential can obtain a token for the supplied scope. The first request's validation error therefore does not prevent disclosure on a later request. Changing the request origin between requests is not required.

Fix

Update to 1.0.1 on the stable release line or 1.1.0-beta.2 on the preview release line.

The fix caches the scope only after challenge resource verification succeeds when verification is enabled. Rejected challenges no longer populate the cache. The existing option to disable challenge resource verification is unchanged; this fix does not add exact-origin binding.
